title: How do monuments shape public memory?
essentialQuestion: How do monuments shape public memory?
learningGoal: Tell an event apart from a later monument to it and from a particular bronze cast, explain how a sculptor's choices shape a public account, and connect a town's commission with what it remembers.

evidence.question: Calais and French public sculpture in the nineteenth century, remembering a siege from the Middle Ages; the two museum bronzes were cast at different times. Look at the whole group first, then at the single figure.

sections.heading: Remembering is a choice made in the present
sections.text:
A monument is made at a particular time to remember something. Its subject may belong to a much earlier period. So studying it involves two historical questions. What is being remembered? And why did later people choose to remember it in this form? The artist, the people who commissioned it, its place and its audience all shape that public account.

In the 1880s, the French town of Calais commissioned a monument from Auguste Rodin. It would commemorate, or publicly remember, citizens linked with the Hundred Years' War. Rodin drew on the medieval writer Jean Froissart's account of the siege of 1347. In that account, six leading citizens offered themselves to England's King Edward III in exchange for the town's protection. Rodin's sculpture shows them setting out, when their fate was uncertain. It is a nineteenth-century interpretation of a medieval story, not an eyewitness record.
sections.simpler:
A monument helps people remember. It may be about a much earlier time. So we ask two questions. What is remembered? And why did later people remember it this way? The artist, the people who paid, the place and the viewers all matter.

In the 1880s, the town of Calais in France asked Rodin for a monument. It would commemorate some of its people from a long war. To commemorate means to remember in public. Rodin used a story by Jean Froissart, a writer from the Middle Ages. In 1347, an army surrounded Calais. Six leading men offered themselves to England's king, Edward III. In return, he would keep the town safe. Rodin shows the men as they leave, not knowing what will happen. He made it more than 500 years later.

sections.heading: Six citizens, side by side
sections.text:
The group has six figures, each with a different gesture and expression. Rodin placed them all on one level instead of raising one above the others. Plain clothes and vulnerable poses make the monument very different from a statue of a victorious ruler on horseback. Here, civic courage, the courage of a town's citizens, appears as people facing a hard choice together. Each one responds in his own way.

The town council had first planned a monument to Eustache de Saint-Pierre, the best-known citizen in the group. By including all six, Rodin shifted attention toward a shared action. This was a choice about public memory as well as composition. Deciding whom to show helped define the story the town would remember in public.

A separate figure, Jean d'Aire, helps us study those decisions. The National Gallery of Art's version shows a clothed man standing firmly and holding a large key. His posture and hands give the figure weight. A whole group and a single study offer different views of the same larger project. Their size and the way they are displayed also affect how an audience meets them.
sections.simpler:
The monument has six men. Each one moves and looks in a different way. Rodin put them all on one level. They wear plain clothes. Their poses look weak, not proud. They are not like a king on a horse. It shows civic courage. Civic means about a town and its people. Here, courage means facing a hard choice together. But each man reacts in his own way.

At first, the town wanted a monument to one man, Eustache de Saint-Pierre. He was the best known of the six. Rodin showed all six instead. So the monument is about a shared act. Choosing whom to show shaped the story the town remembers.

Rodin also made a single figure, Jean d'Aire. A man stands firmly and holds a large key. His body and hands look strong. Their size and how they are shown change how we see them.

sections.heading: An artist's travels and a bronze's dates
sections.text:
Rodin's career also crossed borders. He grew up in a working-class district of Paris and trained in the decorative arts. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 disrupted work, he continued his career in Belgium. A later journey to Italy deepened his interest in Michelangelo's sculpture. Calling Rodin a French artist names an important connection. But his skills developed through particular schools, jobs and travel. Artistic culture was shaped by movement as well as by local institutions.

Dates need particular care with sculpture. A model can be made first, and a bronze cast, an object formed in a mould, can be produced much later. The Met's group was modelled in 1884–95 but cast in 1985. The National Gallery of Art's smaller Jean d'Aire was modelled in 1884–89 and probably cast in 1895. Neither is a bronze made at the time of the medieval event, and each museum object is a separate cast.
sections.simpler:
Rodin's life also crossed borders. He grew up in a part of Paris where working people lived. He learned to make decorations. A war in 1870 and 1871 stopped much of the work, so he worked in Belgium. Later, in Italy, he studied Michelangelo's sculpture. Rodin was French. But his skills came from schools, jobs and travel.

Dates need care with sculpture. First an artist makes a model. Then a bronze cast is made, maybe much later. A cast is made by pouring metal into a mould. The Met's group is from a model made in 1884–95. But it was cast in 1985. The smaller Jean d'Aire is from a model made in 1884–89. It was probably cast in 1895. Neither was made in 1347. Each one is a separate cast.

glossary.definition: A work made to help people remember a person or event.
glossary.example: The town of Calais asked Rodin for a monument.

glossary.definition: Remembering a person or event in public.
glossary.example: The monument was a commemoration of six citizens.

glossary.definition: To do with a town and the people who live in it.
glossary.example: Rodin's monument shows civic courage, not a king's victory.

glossary.definition: An object made by pouring liquid metal into a mould.
glossary.example: The Met's bronze is a cast made in 1985.

write.prompt: Explain how Rodin's monument shows an idea about civic courage. Use one choice you can see and one fact from its past.
sentenceStarters: So the monument shows courage as ...
write.example: Rodin chose to show six citizens on the same level, in plain clothes. Each one has a different gesture, and none of them stands above the others. The history tells us that the town council first wanted a monument to just one man, Eustache de Saint-Pierre. So the monument shows courage as something people share. Each man faces the same hard choice in his own way.

sensitiveNotes: The siege story turns on six citizens offering their lives to save their town, during a war. Keep the account brief and non-graphic, and don't ask for any reenactment or role-play of the threatened people. The Franco-Prussian War is named only as the reason Rodin moved to Belgium for work.
educatorNotes: An old-looking monument is not necessarily from the time of the event it shows. Keep three dates apart: the siege (1347), the model (1884–95, or 1884–89 for Jean d'Aire) and each bronze's casting date (1985 for The Met's group, probably 1895 for the National Gallery of Art's figure).

Answer points for Write: a group of citizens on one level, varied gestures, vulnerability alongside courage; a town commission in the nineteenth century commemorating a much earlier event, and the council's first plan for Eustache de Saint-Pierre alone. Accept other supported readings; don't require a single definition of heroism.

The Froissart-based story, the group composition and the commission come from The Met's educator resource on The Burghers of Calais (PDF, printed pages 11–12 and 16). Its chronology separates the council's decision in 1884 from Rodin's selection in 1885; the reading says "in the 1880s". The Hirshhorn's account confirms the civic commission; its photographs are not open for reuse.

Rodin's background (Paris, decorative-arts training, work in Belgium, Italy) comes from Clare Vincent's essay for The Met, Auguste Rodin (1840–1917). The essay shows adult-themed works elsewhere, so use only that background passage and don't send learners to it unfiltered.

The National Gallery of Art's Jean d'Aire is a reduction (a smaller version) cast probably in 1895, not part of The Met's group or a full-size figure. The Met's group was cast in 1985 by the Coubertin Foundry; keep the cast date in its caption.
changes: 8 November 2026: new lesson, written from Justin's brief Art, Architecture and Society (4 November, expanded 7 November). The standard reading is the brief's, lightly edited for plain words, with Rodin's background moved after the commission so the story of the monument comes first; the simpler reading, key words and tasks follow the brief's vocabulary, Write, Speak and Reflect.
